case.title: The Flood on Bay Street
case.hook: Main Street is fixed. But the same hurricane pushed seawater into every home on Bay Street. The town council gave me three plans and one budget. They want to know which plan to build before the next storm season. I set up a test tank in the lab. Help me run the tests.
case.question: Which plan should the town build, and how can they make it even better?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lab. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: The town’s biggest limit (constraint): the plan must cost $2 million or less.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the test tank
clues.t: In the big storm: sea wall 1 ft of water, living shoreline 2 ft, sand dune 4 ft, no plan 6 ft.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: score the plans
clues.t: The sea wall and the living shoreline each got 2 ✓, but the sea wall costs $4 million: it breaks the limit.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: make it better
clues.t: A sand dune behind the living shoreline cut the water to 1 ft, for $1.5 million in all.

solve.title: Which plan should Bay Street build?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: The sea wall. It kept out the most water in every storm, so it is the best plan for Bay Street.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 3. The sea wall costs $4 million, and the town has $2 million. A plan that breaks a constraint can’t be picked.

options.t: The living shoreline with a sand dune behind it. It fits the budget, helps wildlife, and keeps homes mostly dry.
options.why: Case cracked! You met the goals, stayed inside the limit, and revised the winner. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: The sand dune alone. It is the cheapest plan, so the town should build it and save the rest of the money.
options.why: Check Clue 2. In the big storm, the dune alone let 4 feet of water reach the homes.

judge.afterText: Sort them so we know what a good plan must do
judge.title: Goal or limit?
todo: Read the line from the wish list.
Drag it to a side, or tap a side.
judge.hint: Read the line, then drag it to a side, or tap a side.

why.t: Engineers write down the goals and the limits before they build anything. Then they test every plan against them.

cards.t: Keep seawater out of the homes on Bay Street.
cards.why: That’s what the plan should DO: a goal.
cards.miss: Is this something the plan should do, or a limit on it?

cards.why: Money is a limit: a constraint.
cards.miss: Money is something the town only has so much of.

cards.t: Give fish and birds a place to live.
cards.why: A good plan could also help wildlife: a goal.
cards.miss: Is helping wildlife a thing the plan should do?

cards.t: Be finished before the next hurricane season.
cards.why: Time is a limit: a constraint.
cards.miss: Time is something the town only has so much of.

cards.t: Don’t block the town’s boat ramp.
cards.why: A rule the plan must follow: a constraint.
cards.miss: This is a “must not”. Is that a goal or a limit?

cards.why: How long it lasts is part of how good the plan is: a goal.
cards.miss: Lasting a long time is something a good plan should do.

cards.t: Fit in the 50 feet of land between the water and the homes.
cards.why: Space is a limit: a constraint.
cards.miss: There is only so much land. Is that a goal or a limit?

cards.t: Keep the beach open for families.
cards.why: That’s something the town wants the plan to do: a goal.
cards.miss: Is this something the town wants, or a limit?

judge.win: Clue 1: the town’s biggest limit is money. The plan must cost $2 million or less.

tank.afterText: Watch how much water reaches the homes
tank.title: Shoreline test tank
tank.model: This is a model. The numbers are made up, but they follow what scientists have measured: walls block water, and roots and reefs take energy out of waves.
todo: Pick a plan and a storm.
Press Run the storm and read how much water reaches the homes.
Test the sea wall, the living shoreline, and the sand dune in the big storm.

why.t: A long tank of water where engineers make small waves to test a model of a shore. It lets them try many plans without waiting for a real storm.

score.afterText: Use your test results to score
score.title: Score the plans
todo: Tap ✓ if the plan meets it, or ✗ if it doesn’t.
Score both plans on every row.

why.t: Engineers line up the plans side by side and check each one against the same goals and limits. It keeps the choice fair.

rows.t: Keeps homes mostly dry (1 ft or less) in a big storm
rows.miss: Check your test tank table: how much water reached the homes in the big storm?
Look at the Wildlife column in your table.
Look at the Ready column. Mangroves need time to grow.
Check the cost of each plan in the case file.

score.q: Both plans got 2 ✓. Which one can the town choose?

opts.t: The living shoreline. The sea wall breaks the $2 million limit, and a plan that breaks a constraint can’t be picked.
The sea wall, because it keeps out the most water.
opts.miss: Look at the limit row. Can the town pay $4 million?

opts.t: Neither one. It’s a tie, so they should build nothing.
opts.miss: A tie on goals? Check which plan stays inside the limit.

score.win: Clue 3: both plans got 2 ✓, but the sea wall breaks the $2 million limit. The living shoreline wins.

revise.afterText: Then pick a fix and re-run the big storm
revise.title: Make it better
todo: Pick the living shoreline’s weak spot.
Press Re-run the big storm. Keep trying until the plan meets the goal AND the limit.

why.t: A fix is just a guess until you test it. Engineers test, fix, and test again.

revise.weakQ: The town picked the living shoreline. What is its weak spot?

weak.t: In a big storm, 2 feet of water still reaches the homes.

weak.miss: It costs $1 million. The town has $2 million.
Mangroves and oysters give fish and birds a home.

revise.fixQ: Pick a fix. The town has $2 million in all.

fixes.t: Add a sand dune with sea oats behind the mangroves
fixes.why: Two layers of protection: the mangroves and oysters calm the waves, then the dune stops most of the water. Homes stay mostly dry, it fits the budget, and turtles get a nesting beach.
The homes stay dry, but $5 million breaks the $2 million limit. The town can’t pick it.
A good idea for later! But young mangroves take years to grow, so in the next big storm, 2 feet of water still reaches the homes.

fixes.t: Raise every house on Bay Street
fixes.why: Raised homes stay dry, but $7 million is way over the $2 million limit.

revise.win: Clue 4: a sand dune behind the living shoreline cut the water to 1 foot, for $1.5 million in all.

q1.A: A goal is what the plan should DO. Is a money limit a goal?
q1.C: An effect is a change caused by something. Is this a change?

q2.B: Built mitigation is made by people, like concrete walls. Are mangroves built?
q2.C: Planning mitigation is rules and plans on paper. Are oysters a plan?

q3.B: A constraint is a limit. Did adding a dune set a limit?
q3.C: A hazard is a natural event. Did the engineers make a storm?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how engineers choose a plan?
“But”, “AND” and “no matter” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A plan has to meet the goals and stay inside the limits.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “meet”, “goals”, “inside” and “limits”. Those words carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

welcome.label: Welcome · the flood on Bay Street
welcome.script: June here! Main Street is safe now, but Bay Street had a rough storm. Seawater pushed right into people’s homes. The town council handed me three plans and a budget, and they want an answer before the next hurricane season. Today you’re my engineer. Let’s test those plans.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · goal or limit? (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Here’s the council’s wish list. Before we test anything, we sort it. A goal is something the plan should do. A limit is something the plan has to stay inside, like money, time, or space. Read each line carefully. Some are tricky.

part1.label: Part 1 · the test tank (Clue 2)
part1.script: Welcome to my test tank! Ocean on the left, the town on the right, and your plan in the middle. Pick a plan, pick a storm, and run it. Watch the water at the homes. Make sure you try every plan in the big storm. That’s the one that matters most.

part2.label: Part 2 · score the plans (Clue 3)
part2.script: Now we score the two strongest plans, side by side. Use your test results for each row. Here’s my tip: count the check marks, then look very carefully at the row that says limit.

part3.label: Part 3 · make it better (Clue 4)
part3.script: Every plan has a weak spot. First, find the living shoreline’s weak spot. Then try a fix and re-run the big storm. If your fix breaks the budget, try another one. Engineers never get it perfect the first time.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: All four clues? Then crack the case at the top of this tab: which plan should Bay Street build? After that, answer two questions, write the town an engineering brief, and finish with your CER.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: The council wants to know what makes a good engineering solution. That’s a big question! Think about the sea wall’s price, the living shoreline, and the dune that fixed the weak spot. Pick your claim, tap two pieces of evidence, and explain your thinking.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! Bay Street gets a living shoreline with a dune behind it. It fits the budget, it helps wildlife, and the homes stay mostly dry. You did real engineering today. Good luck on the Unit 4 test. You’ve got this.
